thesis: The history of social norms research can be read as a series of responses to inconsistent evidence about the norm–behavior relationship, each specifying more precisely which norms, perceived by whom and under what conditions, guide behavior.

A decade later, Rimal and Lapinski (2015) re-explicated social norms, reaffirming their central assumption that “at their core, norms are communication phenomena” (p. 393) and treating norms as dynamic, both shaping and shaped by human action. They also proposed that collective norms are likely one driver of perceived descriptive norms and that communication strengthens this link, a hypothesis they noted had not yet been tested.

(2006) used social judgment theory to measure students’ latitudes of acceptance, noncommitment, and rejection for normative information, which differed in believability, and argued that a campaign built on a true norm in the latitude of noncommitment would likely be effective. Taken together, each step in this history can be read as a response to mixed evidence about the norm–behavior relationship.

These syntheses indicate that findings on the norm–behavior relationship remain mixed, and culturally based differences in the effectiveness of norm appeals (Liu & Lapinski, 2024) point to culture as one source of that variation.
open: Theories of social norms were developed largely with U.S. and European samples, and none directly accounts for cultural dynamics in normative influence (Lapinski et al., 2022). Research on cultural dynamics has studied co-cultural groups within national boundaries and compared countries (Liu et al., 2022). In this essay, cultural dynamics refers to (a) variation in normative influence across such groups and countries and (b) the processes through which culture is expected to shape normative influence. Culture may affect how norms are conceptualized, how much weight they carry in decisions relative to other influences, and the psychosocial dynamics through which they operate (Lapinski et al., 2022). Studies have located culture in the nation, in the individual, and, least often, in the group whose norms are studied.
A: First, culture has been located in the nation. Commonly, nationality serves as a proxy for culture. For example, the same norm appeals shifted the targeted perceptions more in a Chinese than in a U.S. student sample, as the authors had predicted from differences in tightness, institutional signals, and message interpretation (Liu & Lapinski, 2024). None of these differences was measured, and the samples also differed in survey mode. Alternatively, a cultural dimension is scored at the level of the nation, as in Gelfand et al.’s (2011) tightness–looseness scores for 33 nations. Such scores can be examined across studies, as in a post hoc analysis in which Hofstede’s dimensions did not explain variation in the descriptive–injunctive norm correlation (Kalny et al., 2026). Both approaches locate culture at the level of the nation, whereas country and culture are incongruent under most conditions because co-cultural groups share national identities (Liu et al., 2022).
B: Second, Lapinski et al. (2007) measured cultural orientation in individuals in response to the criticism that work on individualism–collectivism makes “broad generalizations about people from different countries” (p. 135), an approach that later studies have followed (Liu & Lapinski, 2024, 2025; Yoon et al., 2024). Group orientation, the extent to which group goals prevail over individual goals, is distinct from group identity, the TNSB moderator that refers to similarity with and aspiration toward a specific referent group (Lapinski et al., 2007; Rimal & Real, 2005). Group-oriented participants held positive water conservation attitudes and intentions regardless of perceived prevalence, which was negatively associated with both among the individualistically oriented (Lapinski et al., 2007). Group orientation was directly associated with physical distancing, but the relationships between perceived norms and distancing were steeper at lower levels of group orientation (Yoon et al., 2024). It also predicted intentions to prevent food waste without moderating the effects of norm appeals (Liu & Lapinski, 2024). For behaviors that benefit the collective, then, the group-oriented have been no more, and sometimes less, dependent on normative information than the individualistically oriented. In Chinese and U.S. adults, stating sanctions explicitly added to an injunctive appeal only among people who preferred low-context communication, and higher perceived cultural tightness strengthened some effects of injunctive appeals while weakening others (Liu & Lapinski, 2025).
C_before_fn: Third, culture has been treated as the context that defines what a norm is. Liu et al. (2022) proposed a model for culturally contextualized measurement, in which concepts and items are developed through formative work within a cultural group, including interviews, before they are tested, and applied it with ethnically Tibetan pastoralists in Western China.
C_after_fn: In interviews, herding decisions were constrained by ecological, market, and policy forces, explicit communication about norms arose mainly when problems or policy changes occurred, and sanctions for deviation were implied rather than stated (Lapinski et al., 2022). Injunctive norms were therefore defined without sanctions (Liu et al., 2022), a departure from definitions that make sanctions the primary difference between injunctive and descriptive norms (Lapinski & Rimal, 2005).
D: Across these approaches, the processes through which culture is expected to alter normative influence, such as the detection of implied sanctions (Liu & Lapinski, 2025) or motivations to comply (Rimal & Lapinski, 2015), have been proposed more often than tested directly. None of the studies reviewed here manipulated culture.

fn_sna: The social norms approach is a normative restructuring strategy that seeks to change behavior by changing perceptions of a behavior’s prevalence among one’s social referents (Lapinski et al., 2007), as in campus programs that report the actual prevalence of student drinking. It originated in Perkins and Berkowitz’s (1986) finding that students overestimate their peers’ drinking.
